items.q: In the FAST examination, where is the right upper quadrant view obtained?
o: Below the xiphoid over the liver
Between the liver and the right kidney at Morison pouch
At the spleen beside the left kidney
Behind the bladder in the pelvis
items.exp: Free blood settles in the hepatorenal recess, so the probe looks at Morison pouch for a black stripe there. Guideline: ACEP emergency ultrasound guideline, section on the FAST examination.

items.q: What does a black anechoic stripe in Morison pouch mean in trauma?
o: Free fluid likely blood in the peritoneum
items.exp: Fresh blood is echo free and collects in the dependent recess, so a black stripe there means free fluid until proven otherwise. Guideline: ACEP emergency ultrasound guideline, section on free fluid.

items.q: In the FAST examination, where is the left upper quadrant view obtained?
o: Between the liver and the right kidney
Between the spleen and the left kidney at the splenorenal recess
items.exp: The left dependent recess lies beside the spleen, so fluid from splenic injury appears between spleen and kidney. Guideline: ACEP emergency ultrasound guideline, section on the FAST examination.

items.q: In the FAST examination, where is the pelvic view obtained?
o: Behind the bladder at the rectovesical or Douglas pouch
items.exp: The pelvis is the lowest recess when supine, so fluid appears behind the bladder in male patients or behind the uterus in female patients. Guideline: ACEP emergency ultrasound guideline, section on the FAST examination.

items.q: In the FAST examination, what does the subxiphoid cardiac view look for?
o: A black echo free space around the heart meaning pericardial fluid
items.exp: Blood in the pericardium appears as a black space around the moving heart, which explains shock after chest trauma. Guideline: ACEP emergency ultrasound guideline, section on pericardial fluid.

items.q: Fresh free blood on FAST appears black, but older clotted blood looks brighter. Why does this matter?
o: Clot can be missed if the scan is delayed after injury
Bright areas always mean bowel gas
Brightness proves the scan is normal
items.exp: Clot becomes echogenic with time and blends with tissue, so a late scan can underread bleeding and serial scans help. Guideline: ACEP emergency ultrasound guideline, section on pitfalls.

items.q: Which probe suits the FAST abdominal views best?
o: Low frequency curvilinear probe for depth
items.exp: The abdomen needs depth, so a low frequency curvilinear probe with a wide near view reaches the recesses. Guideline: ACEP emergency ultrasound guideline, section on equipment.

items.q: A FAST scan is negative but the patient remains unstable with abdominal injury. What next?
o: Repeat the scan and continue resuscitation with surgical review
items.exp: Small or fresh bleeds can be missed early, so an unstable patient needs serial scanning with the surgical team involved. Guideline: ACEP emergency ultrasound guideline, section on serial examination.

items.q: In lung ultrasound, what does lung sliding with A lines mean?
o: Normal aerated lung with the pleura opposed
items.exp: Sliding shows visceral on parietal pleura with reverberation lines, which is the normal pattern in an aerated lung. Guideline: International lung ultrasound consensus (WINFOCUS), section on normal lung.

items.q: Absent lung sliding with a barcode sign on M mode suggests what?
o: Pneumothorax with air separating the pleural layers
items.exp: M mode shows a flat barcode when no sliding moves the line, which fits air in the pleural space. Guideline: International lung ultrasound consensus (WINFOCUS), section on pneumothorax.

items.q: What is the lung point in extended FAST?
o: The border where sliding returns beside absent sliding
items.exp: A visible transition between sliding and no sliding marks the edge of the pneumothorax and confirms it. Guideline: International lung ultrasound consensus (WINFOCUS), section on pneumothorax confirmation.

items.q: Multiple B lines in both lungs with poor oxygenation suggest what?
o: Interstitial fluid as in pulmonary oedema
items.exp: B lines are vertical tails from wet septa, so diffuse bilateral B lines fit interstitial fluid rather than air. Guideline: International lung ultrasound consensus (WINFOCUS), section on interstitial syndrome.

items.q: What does the seashore sign on M mode lung imaging show?
o: Normal lung with granular sand below the pleural line
items.exp: Motion below the pleural line gives a sandy grain, so the seashore pattern confirms sliding at that point. Guideline: International lung ultrasound consensus (WINFOCUS), section on M mode signs.

items.q: Where is fluid sought at the PLAPS point in lung ultrasound?
o: Above the diaphragm at the dependent pleural recess
items.exp: The posterolateral point looks at the costophrenic recess, where pleural fluid collects when supine. Guideline: International lung ultrasound consensus (WINFOCUS), section on pleural effusion.

items.q: How is the inferior vena cava measured for volume assessment?
o: Diameter near the right atrium with sniff collapse noted
items.exp: Size plus collapse with a sniff reflects right atrial pressure, so the long axis cut near the atrium is the standard site. Guideline: ASE right heart quantification guideline, section on inferior vena cava and right atrial pressure.

items.q: An IVC of 24 mm with less than 20 percent collapse on sniff suggests what?
o: High right atrial pressure around 15 mmHg
items.exp: A large vein that barely collapses means the right atrium is full, which reads as high pressure rather than empty. Guideline: ASE right heart quantification guideline, section on inferior vena cava and right atrial pressure.

items.q: An IVC of 14 mm with more than 50 percent collapse on sniff suggests what?
o: Low right atrial pressure near 0 to 5 mmHg
items.exp: A small vein that collapses well means low filling pressure, which fits an empty rather than overloaded right atrium. Guideline: ASE right heart quantification guideline, section on inferior vena cava and right atrial pressure.

items.q: IVC assessment fails in a patient with high abdominal pressure. What is the limitation?
o: Raised abdominal pressure distends the vein whatever the volume state
The vein is always normal then
items.exp: External pressure keeps the vein full, so size and collapse no longer track right atrial pressure fairly. Guideline: ASE right heart quantification guideline, section on limitations.

items.q: In the BLUE protocol, an A profile with a leg clot suggests what?
o: Pulmonary embolism as the cause of breathlessness
items.exp: A dry lung pattern with proven venous thrombosis points to embolism rather than wet lung or air leak. Guideline: International lung ultrasound consensus (WINFOCUS), section on BLUE profiles.

items.q: In the BLUE protocol, diffuse B lines with preserved sliding suggest what?
items.exp: Bilateral wet lines with sliding fit fluid filled septa, which is the oedema pattern rather than absent sliding. Guideline: International lung ultrasound consensus (WINFOCUS), section on BLUE profiles.

items.q: In the BLUE protocol, absent sliding with A lines on one side suggests what?
items.exp: Dry lines without sliding on one side fit air in that pleural space, with the other side acting as control. Guideline: International lung ultrasound consensus (WINFOCUS), section on BLUE profiles.

items.q: In the BLUE protocol, a C profile with anterior consolidation suggests what?
items.exp: Anterior tissue like liver with air bronchograms means consolidated lung, which fits infection rather than oedema. Guideline: International lung ultrasound consensus (WINFOCUS), section on BLUE profiles.

items.q: In the RUSH protocol, what does the pump step assess?
o: Contractility, chamber size and pericardial fluid
items.exp: Pump looks at the heart as the cause of shock, so poor squeeze or tamponade found here changes care at once. Guideline: ACEP emergency ultrasound guideline, section on shock ultrasound.

items.q: In the RUSH protocol, what does the tank step assess?
o: Volume state from cava, FAST fluid and lung water
items.exp: Tank judges fullness and leaks, so cava size, free fluid and lung B lines together guide fluids. Guideline: ACEP emergency ultrasound guideline, section on shock ultrasound.

items.q: In the RUSH protocol, what does the pipes step assess?
o: Aorta for aneurysm or dissection and veins for clot
items.exp: Pipes checks the vessels carrying flow, so a dilated aorta or a non compressible vein explains shock fast. Guideline: ACEP emergency ultrasound guideline, section on shock ultrasound.

items.q: A shocked patient has a flat small cava, dry lungs and no free fluid. What does RUSH suggest?
o: Empty tank needing fluids with ongoing review
items.exp: An empty collapsible cava with dry lungs and no leak means volume loss until proven otherwise, so fluids with review fit. Guideline: ACEP emergency ultrasound guideline, section on shock ultrasound.

items.q: During cardiac arrest, when is the echo probe applied?
o: During the 10 second pulse check without pausing compressions longer
items.exp: Compressions must restart within 10 seconds, so the subxiphoid view is gained and lost inside that pause. Guideline: ACEP emergency ultrasound guideline, section on cardiac arrest echo.

items.q: Arrest echo shows organised cardiac motion without a pulse. What is this?
o: Pseudo pulseless electrical activity with possible reversible cause
items.exp: Visible motion means the heart still moves, so reversible causes must be sought rather than stopping at once. Guideline: ACEP emergency ultrasound guideline, section on cardiac arrest echo.

items.q: Arrest echo shows a large pericardial collection with chamber collapse. What is the next step?
o: Urgent pericardial drainage with ongoing resuscitation
items.exp: Tamponade blocks filling, so draining the sac during resuscitation can restore output where drugs alone cannot. Guideline: ACEP emergency ultrasound guideline, section on pericardial tamponade.

items.q: Arrest echo shows a dilated poorly moving right ventricle with a flat septum. What should be considered?
o: Massive pulmonary embolism with thrombolysis considered per protocol
items.exp: Acute right heart strain in arrest fits large embolism, so protocol based thrombolysis is weighed with the team. Guideline: ACEP emergency ultrasound guideline, section on right heart strain.

items.q: Pleural fluid on ultrasound appears as what?
o: A black anechoic space above the diaphragm with lung floating inside
items.exp: Fluid transmits sound well and looks black, so the compressed lung is seen moving within it above the diaphragm. Guideline: International lung ultrasound consensus (WINFOCUS), section on pleural effusion.

items.q: Why is the curvilinear probe chosen for abdominal POCUS in adults?
o: It is only for the eye
Low frequency reaches deep with a wide near view
items.exp: Deep recesses need penetration and a wide footprint, which the low frequency curved probe provides. Guideline: ACEP emergency ultrasound guideline, section on equipment.

items.q: What must be recorded for every emergency ultrasound study?
o: Images with findings and interpretation in the notes
items.exp: Saved images with a written read make the study reviewable and safe, so documentation is part of every scan. Guideline: ACEP emergency ultrasound guideline, section on documentation.

items.q: Free fluid in the pelvis of a young woman with a positive pregnancy test raises concern for what?
o: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy needing urgent review
items.exp: Blood in the Douglas pouch with pregnancy of unknown site fits rupture, so urgent gynaecology review follows. Guideline: ACEP emergency ultrasound guideline, section on pelvic fluid.

items.q: FAST shows free fluid and the patient stays unstable despite resuscitation. What does the protocol say?
o: Discharge with review in one week
Repeat FAST only after one day
Urgent surgical review for the operating theatre
items.exp: Positive fluid with instability means bleeding needing control, so the surgical team and theatre come first. Guideline: ACEP emergency ultrasound guideline, section on positive FAST.

items.q: A trauma patient has absent left lung sliding after a line insertion. What is the likely cause?
items.exp: A new air leak after needling above the clavicle fits pleural puncture, so bedside lung scan confirms it fast. Guideline: International lung ultrasound consensus (WINFOCUS), section on procedure related pneumothorax.
